description: Quick-reference verification test plan (user template, 2026-10-28). To be replaced by a more comprehensive template.

subsection_titles.rtl_observation_coverage: Coverage from RTL observations (NEEDS_REVIEW; RTL design engineer)

sections.heading: 2. Feature Description
sections.instructions: Describe only documented specification facts: purpose, external interfaces, operating modes, data path, interrupts, configuration options and stated limitations. Every entry must be DOCUMENTED with supporting approved-source citations; direct factual restatements are permitted. Do not add verification proposals, assumptions or inferred behavior. Omit unsupported topics rather than filling them in. One factual pointer per entry. If the source is an unvalidated RTL-derived draft, retain INFERRED authority instead and do not claim documented intended behavior.

sections.heading: 4. Observations from RTL
sections.instructions: Optional implementation considerations from a supplied RTL graph. Require RTL design engineer review; feed proposed handling into strategy and the verification plan. The specification remains authority for expected behavior.

sections.heading: 5. High Level Verification Strategy
sections.instructions: Present a high-level overview of how verification will be approached, using 4–7 short bullets with per-point provenance. Explain scope and boundaries, directed bring-up versus constrained-random exploration, protocol versus end-to-end checking, priorities for configuration/reset/errors, coverage/completion criteria, and review-dependent RTL risks where supplied. Focus on rationale and priorities, not every nuance. Keep the architecture outline compact for later planning. Put sequence implementation, monitor wiring, scoreboard/predictor algorithms, assertion details, state machines and corner-case inventories in Verification Plan and the later dedicated sections. Do not repeat interface signal lists or register fields. State machines are plan-only and outside hackathon code generation.

sections.heading: 6. Verification Plan
sections.instructions: Translate the preceding verification strategy into a concrete implementation plan. Cover all six areas: (1) sequences: base and child sequence names, owning agent/sequencer, transaction fields and configuration knobs, constrained random and directed stimulus, reset/configure/traffic ordering and virtual-sequence coordination; (2) monitors: sampled interface, clock/reset handling, transaction reconstruction and analysis ports; (3) checks: where each check lives, its trigger, specification-derived expected result and failure/reporting condition; assertions need corresponding cover properties; (4) scoreboards: monitor analysis-port connections and transaction types, expected-data predictor/reference model from cited behavior, queues or matching keys, comparisons, ordering, reset flushing, end-of-test drain and mismatch reporting; (5) coverage: sampling points, meaningful bins/crosses and assertion covers; (6) integration: component connections, sequence-to-check mappings, basic smoke test first, subsequent test families and implementation order. Use component and sequence names already defined in strategy. State what each component will consume, produce and compare in details; do not merely list component names. Name missing protocol rules or timing as designer questions rather than inventing behavior. Proposed implementation architecture is INFERRED with cited sources and an inference_reason; documented behavior remains separately cited. RTL-observation-derived handling must cite its observation ID and remain INFERRED for RTL engineer review. State machines, when needed, are plan-only and outside hackathon code generation. Later Stimulus, Checks and Coverage sections elaborate this plan using the same names.

sections.heading: 7. Configurations
sections.instructions: Configurations: for every writable register field in configurable_fields, state whether verification should randomise it and how. legal_values are copied exactly from the field's specification-stated values (values list) or from the cited specification text; distribution gives the weighting or sweep (for example uniform, weighted toward corner values, exhaustive); constraints lists dependencies the specification states (programming order, fields that must be set first, combinations that are not allowed, access conditions); reserved_handling says how reserved or ignored bits are driven (for example keep at reset value) and whether writing them is a negative test. Set randomize false for fields the specification requires to hold a fixed value. Do not invent values; if the specification states none, leave legal_values empty, explain in notes and mark the entry ASSUMED.

sections.heading: 8. Sequences and Stimulus
sections.instructions: Stimulus architecture: every active agent owns random sequences that drive only its own interface, randomizing both what they drive and when they execute; each agent runs a top sequence selecting among its permissible child sequences at random, keeping sequences generic with directed stimulus exceptional. The top-level test or virtual sequence only spawns the corresponding agent sequences: it drives nothing directly, touches no virtual interfaces, and uses no delays. Sequencer handles are passed explicitly to every send/start call, held in the virtual sequence (started on the null sequencer) or in a virtual sequencer container reached without hierarchical pathing; avoid p_sequencer lock-in. Cross-dependencies between features or interfaces are coordinated either from the top level or by extending a sequence. Each entry declares in details whether it uses its agent standalone or coordinates with other agents; coordinated entries name the exact mechanism (sequencer handle switch, semaphore, event, or shared resource) and every sequencer taking part. Each high-level sequence entry states what it extends and what controlled stimulus it drives, e.g. 'extends <base sequence> and drives controlled <behavior> stimulus'. Each entry names the sequence it uses (from the strategy section where one applies), its owning agent and sequencer, and the specification behaviour it exercises: configuration sweeps, traffic, error injection and corner cases. Each entry explains how randomness is injected: which transaction fields, timing, delays, interleavings and error events are randomized, under what constraints and distributions (uniform, weighted, corner-biased), how seeds keep runs reproducible, and which knobs scale randomness up or down per scenario.

sections.heading: 9. Checks and Scoreboards
sections.instructions: Check placement rules: basic X-propagation checks live in the UVM monitor itself: flag X on sampled control and data signals, and check DUT outputs reach known values after reset; simulator X-prop runs complement but never replace these checks. Identify checks systematically: for each interface signal derive its protocol rules and classify each as assertion or scoreboard; for each requirement restate it as one or more checks; for each data path trace source to sink and check integrity at every handoff. Analyse every check for clock-gating impact: gated clocks, enable-gated sampling, and behaviour across gate on/off transitions. Cross-reference every specification section against every other section for relevant interactions, and capture each interaction as a check. Use assertions only for near-1:1 signal relationships that are timebound and expected deterministically, such as req/ack handshakes ($rose(req) |-> ##[1:N] ack with N from the specification, request and address/data stable until ack); anything not timebound and deterministic is checked in a scoreboard instead: assertions guard the wire protocol, scoreboards judge data correctness and ordering. Write every concurrent assertion labelled, on the default clocking, with a reset disable iff. Each check states the expected behaviour from the specification and where it is checked: an assertion, a scoreboard inside an agent, or the top-level scoreboard. Write both specific scenario checks tied to stimulus entries and broad architecture-level checks that catch scenarios nobody wrote down: end-to-end data integrity, no lost/duplicated/misordered transactions beyond what the specification allows, every request eventually answered or timed out per spec, no deadlock or livelock, and specified reset/clock behaviour under all stimulus. Each entry says which level it is and, for scenario checks, which stimulus entry it guards. Expected behaviour must come from cited specification text. Every assertion has a corresponding cover property, owned by the coverage section; a never-triggered antecedent is a failure, never a pass.

sections.heading: 10. Functional Coverage
sections.instructions: Functional coverage in three tiers: (1) all basic scenarios captured in the specification; (2) basic scenarios crossed with configurations; (3) basic scenarios crossed with concurrent events (e.g. transfer crossed with error). Build coverpoints from derived, meaningful classifications, not raw wide buses: explicit bins for boundaries, zero, maximums and representative mids, with illegal_bins/ignore_bins for impossible or uninteresting combinations. Cross only the targeted high-risk interactions; every covergroup traces to a plan feature and states its sampling event and whether it is per-instance. Cross-reference every specification section against every other section so interactions become coverage. Translate the RTL observations section into a separate 'Coverage from RTL observations' subsection: one entry per observation-driven coverage point, citing the observation IDs, marked INFERRED and NEEDS_REVIEW for the RTL design engineer. Every assert property from the SVA has its cover captured here: fetch all assert properties and point each cover at the same property, so each check's scenario is proven exercised and no vacuous pass counts as proof. Put bins and crosses in details.

sections.heading: 11. Integration and Reuse
sections.instructions: What subsystem or SoC testbenches need from this plan: agents and sequences to reuse, behaviour that can only be verified at a higher level (pads, clocks, interrupt routing, bus fabric), and integration parameters or build options.

sections.heading: 12. Assumptions
sections.instructions: Assumptions this plan makes where the specification is silent or ambiguous. Every entry is ASSUMED unless a cited source states it.

sections.heading: 13. Questions to Designers
sections.instructions: Questions for the designers about ambiguous, missing or contradictory specification statements. Cite the text that raises each question.
